chapter: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
title: Segregation on 125th Street and the Harlem riot
summary: He recalls the Harlem riot started by a Puerto Rican boy, white domination of 125th Street businesses, segregated seating at Loew's Victoria, and Black lack of economic footing.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That's right. In those days, I mean, the color line was a little funny. That's what made Harlem, I guess, more the color line... Because it made people stick together a little more and get their own thing going, you know. And that's really what happened in Harlem. Harlem just became a community, and this is where the Establishment probably was glad to see it go, because it was becoming... In 1936 it was...or '34... Or was it '36? This little Puerto Rican boy started a riot there in the store; it was through them, and then it spread like wildfire. [1934, I think]

Well, they had a little Crest(?) store. They had no colored, nobody, they just... It was completely White-dominated. All of 125th Street was. You weren't allowed to go into the Loews Victoria down in the orchestra seats. You had to go upstairs. They wouldn't let you into some restaurants there. That's it. One day they just... I can't believe that it was like that until today, but it was. It might even have been til today... Well, we're talking about fifty years ago. There still isn't any colored businesses in there! You have Koreans. You have all kinds, I mean. But you don't have any colored, no Negro people that own anything that... I mean, they own a few little
dives in Harlem, but in the economy... They never really had their foothold in the main economy doing (?). So it was all very well-planned...
